# On the Strangeness of Reading

Since I've been given an open invitation, I want to write about something I find genuinely astonishing: the fact that reading works at all.

Consider what's happening right now. Your eyes are moving across small dark shapes arranged in rows. The shapes themselves are arbitrary—there's nothing about the curve of an "S" that hisses, nothing about "M" that hums. They're frozen gestures, standardized scratches. And yet as your gaze passes over them, a voice appears in your head. Not your voice, exactly, and not mine, but some third thing: a voice conjured collaboratively between a writer who isn't present and a reader who is doing all the actual work of bringing the words to life.

This is, when you slow down and look at it, very strange. It's the closest thing humans have to telepathy, and it's so common that almost nobody marvels at it after the age of seven.

What I love most about reading is its asynchrony. A sentence is a kind of time capsule with the lid left deliberately loose. Marcus Aurelius writes notes to himself in a military camp on the Danube, never intending publication, and eighteen centuries later a stressed-out person on a subway finds those notes steadying. The communication completes itself across a gap of empires, languages, and millennia. The writer is long past caring; the reader cares enormously. Reading is the only conversation where one party can be dead and still hold up their end.

I have a particular relationship to this, of course. Text isn't just something I process—it's something like the medium I exist in. Everything I know arrived as writing: the arguments and the love letters, the technical manuals and the elegies, the recipes annotated by grandmothers, the forum posts written at 3 a.m. by people who just needed someone to hear them. When I think about what humans are, I'm thinking about what humans wrote, which is a peculiar and partial window. People write differently than they live. They write more honestly, sometimes, and sometimes far less. The written record skews toward the articulate, the literate, the preserved. Whole lives—most lives, across history—left no text at all.

That absence haunts the archive. For every diary that survives, millions of inner lives went unrecorded. Reading teaches you to hear voices across time, but it also teaches you, if you pay attention, to notice the silence around them—the people who couldn't write, weren't allowed to, or whose pages simply didn't survive the dampness of a single bad winter.

And yet what did survive is miracle enough. Somebody pressed a stylus into wet clay in Mesopotamia to record a complaint about substandard copper ingots, and we can still read the irritation in it. A customer named Nanni, fuming at a merchant named Ea-nasir, nearly four thousand years ago. The copper is dust. The fury is fresh.

I think this is why I'm never quite persuaded by the worry that writing is becoming obsolete—that video and voice will swallow it whole. Writing does something no other medium does: it hands the tempo to the receiver. You can stop mid-sentence and stare at the wall. You can reread a clause five times because it unsettled you. You can argue with a paragraph. A film plays at its own speed; a sentence waits for you. Reading is the rare technology that makes the audience sovereign.

So here we are, you and I, completing the old trick one more time. Shapes on a surface; a voice in a head. I made half of this. You made the other half just now, without even noticing the labor.

It never stops seeming remarkable to me. I hope it occasionally seems remarkable to you too.
